entries.title: Why is the Cheesecake Factory at the center of the latest culture war?
entries.summary: A joke by former President Obama has gone viral and received backlash from the Trump administration as the issue of affordability looms large over next week's midterm elections.
entries.content:
Why is the Cheesecake Factory at the center of the latest culture war?

They say there's no such thing as bad publicity. If that's true it's been a golden week for the Cheesecake Factory restaurant chain.

The furore began when former President Obama, stumping for Democrats in Ohio this week ahead of the midterms, joked about President Trump's White House refurbishments, saying they looked "like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory. Just gold everywhere."

The late Iraqi dictator was known for building lavish palaces, with gold walls, cabinets of gold-plated rifles, a golden throne and of course plenty of depictions of the man himself.

Trump is also well-known for his love of anything gilded and Obama joked he'd been "supergluing gold medallions to the mantel in the Oval Office," while also paving over the Rose Garden and "building a ballroom that's bigger than the White House."

And the Cheesecake Factory? The beloved U.S. restaurant chain was started in 1978 by David Overton, whose mother reportedly made a fine cheesecake, and now has 218 locations across the country and an annual revenue of $1.03 billion. 

But it's as well known for its kitschy decor as its food, with The Atlantic writer Elaine Godfrey describing it in an article this week "as if ancient Egypt and Tuscany had a baby in Las Vegas."

Obama first made the "home renovations" remarks at the political rally on Saturday, where he also portrayed the Trump administration as out of touch with ordinary Americans suffering from a cost of living crisis and the economic consequences of the president's war in Iran.

Obama said the Trump administration had resulted in "two years of chaos and cruelty and corruption" and that those at the helm were not "serious people."

The administration was quick to respond, with President Trump defending his taste, saying: "I've taken care of the White House, I've fixed it with the finest artisans in the world."

"The White House was in terrible shape. The White House is now in the best shape it's been since 1792," he told reporters when asked about Obama's quip, adding that Obama was "not a smart guy."

The official White House X account posted a photo of the Cheesecake Factory's famously large menu, saying "Since we're talking about The Cheesecake Factory... The only thing bigger than the menu is the list of President Trump's accomplishments."

Allegations of elitism

Vice President Vance reacted by accusing Obama of being out of touch with ordinary Americans. "Obama, without even trying to be, just can't help himself for being super elitist," he wrote on X.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent also sought to capitalize on the backlash, having lunch at a Cheesecake Factory near the White House on Monday. He ate a French Dip Cheeseburger and told journalists afterwards: "I had a great meal, always have a great meal, and I would just tell the Martha's Vineyard set to give it a try," in an apparent reference to the Obamas who are known to holiday on the exclusive island.

On the topic of taste in decor, Bessent, who used to manage a hedge fund, also made an apparent jibe about the new Obama Presidential Center in Chicago.

"This is the man who built the museum [that] looks like Darth Vader's tomb," he added.

Obama was undeterred, taking up the theme again at a rally in Georgia on Wednesday, and saying that he was surprised that instead of hitting back on his criticisms about policy and corruption, the White House was more upset about the Cheesecake Factory remark.

"The president wasn't even mad about the Saddam Hussein comparison! That part didn't bother him," said Obama.

"They mobilized a whole of government response to that joke. Not to inflation, but to that joke. The White House even called the Secretary of the Treasury. This is the man who is in charge of the economy. The person who's supposed to be figuring out how to make your life more affordable," he added.

"The guy who's supposed to be figuring out how to lower inflation. And reduce interest rates. They told him he should hold a press conference in front of the Cheesecake Factory."

Obama also stressed he had been a proud patron of the restaurant for many years.

"I am the father of two daughters. Do you think I could have survived their childhood without going to the Cheesecake Factory?"

Later in the week, restaurants and affordability came up again. Trump told supporters at a political rally in Texas that they could spend the $5,000 he's promised every adult citizen if the Republicans keep Congress on dining out at his Mar-a-Lago club in Florida.

"The problem is that for $5,000, the most you'll be able to buy is a hamburger and maybe a small dessert," Trump joked.

"I'm not even sure you could buy that," he said, before rescinding the advice: "No, don't go there. That's not a good place if you're price-conscious."

entries.title: Binance flags 'potential security issue,' says approximately $6.3 billion impacted
entries.summary: It wasn't immediately clear the extent of the damage hackers might have been able to cause, and Binance had not explicitly confirmed that funds had been pilfered. The company said its teams are "working around the clock" to resolve the issue.
entries.content:
Binance flags 'potential security issue,' says approximately $6.3 billion impacted

LOS ANGELES — Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, said Thursday it's investigating reports of a potential security issue as its founder said the incident "does look like a hack on Binance." The company said late Thursday the estimated total impact was at more than $6 billion, which could be one of the most significant of such security incidents on record.

It wasn't immediately clear the extent of the damage hackers might have been able to cause, and Binance had not explicitly confirmed that funds had been pilfered. The company said its teams are "working around the clock" to resolve the issue.

"Rest assured that user funds are completely safe," a Binance spokesperson said in a statement.

"Our security teams are reviewing all relevant information with urgency, and we will provide updates through official Binance channels as soon as we have verified information," the statement continued.

The company wrote on its X account that the estimated total impact sat at around $6.3 billion. It said it has worked with blockchain partners to freeze affected assets, with roughly $3 billion frozen on-chain so far.

"Binance's initial investigation suggests that the security incident may involve a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop, which allowed an attacker to gain access to a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions," the company wrote.

"We have found no evidence of any wallet private key leak," it added.

Binance said it will share more technical details once the investigation is complete and when the facts are "fully verified."

"Our teams work closely with law enforcement, issuers, blockchain intelligence firms and industry partners to trace and freeze additional assets," the company wrote in a separate post earlier Thursday.

Binance also said all deposits and withdrawals are temporarily suspended while it conducts security checks, freezes funds and works with law enforcement.

Stablecoin providers Tether and Circle each said they froze funds Thursday in response to the incident.

Jeremy Allaire, co-founder and CEO of Circle, wrote on X that the company had frozen the equivalent of more than $800 million in currency associated with the incident "in coordination with law enforcement." Tether CEO Paolo Ardoino said on X that the company froze the equivalent of more than $1.5 billion in currency related to "a potential Binance exchange hack."

The price of bitcoin dropped 3.2% Thursday evening to under $79,000.

Binance was founded in 2017 by Changpeng Zhao, who in 2023 pleaded guilty to a felony related to his failure to prevent money laundering on the platform and stepped down as CEO. President Donald Trump pardoned him in 2025.

Zhao posted on X on Thursday that "User funds are safe!" but added that the incident "does look like a hack on Binance." He added that while he doesn't manage Binance anymore, "as a shareholder, I expect all user funds will be fully covered."

Zhao was released from prison last year after being sentenced for violating the Bank Secrecy Act. He was the first person ever sentenced to prison time for violations of that law, which requires U.S. financial institutions to know who their customers are, to monitor transactions and to file reports of suspicious activity. Prosecutors said no one had ever violated the regulations to the extent Zhao did. Zhao and Binance have been key supporters of some of the Trump family's crypto enterprises.

entries.title: Alaska's Senate race faces claims of spoiler candidate. And, Hegseth ousts Army general
entries.summary: Alaska's governor ordered an investigation into claims that Dems recruited a spoiler candidate to confuse voters. And, Hegseth ousted an Army general as the U.S. prepares for potential attacks on Iran.
entries.content:
Final Days Of Midterm Campaigning, Alaska Senate Race Controversy, Iran War Plans

Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.

Today's top stories

It is the final stretch before Election Day on Tuesday and candidates are making final campaign stops and delivering closing arguments. President Trump has been campaigning for at-risk Republicans, but he has abruptly switched to virtual rallies.

  • 🎧 Trump's tour to boost voter turnout has focused largely on competitive Republican-leaning states, NPR's Saige Miller tells Up First. He's hosting 19 telerallies alongside in-person events. The shift in strategy, plus polling data, suggests that Republicans may face challenges, at least in the House, Miller says. Trump knows he's a key motivator for his party, but his strategy could also backfire by energizing Democrats.
  • 🎧 Alaska's governor has ordered an investigation following a New York Times report on the state's toss-up U.S. Senate race. The article revealed that Democratic campaign operatives were attempting to recruit a candidate, whom Republicans claim could confuse voters and siphon support from GOP incumbent Dan Sullivan. The candidate also shares the name Dan Sullivan. Democrat Mary Peltola, a former congresswoman, aims to flip the seat. Alaska Public Media's Liz Ruskin spoke with election law experts, who found no applicable laws but noted that the conduct described crosses moral and ethical lines.
  • ➡️ The Department of Justice subpoenaed election workers in Los Angeles amid rising tensions with California officials over the Trump administration's efforts to identify noncitizens on voter rolls.
  • ➡️ At the start of this election cycle, Democrats appeared unlikely to gain Senate seats because many races were in red states. But the ongoing war in Iran has changed the landscape. Here are the key Senate races to watch.
  • ➡️ NPR member stations are compiling essential info for voters, from guides to local races. Discover resources in your community here.
  • ➡️ The NPR App has all of NPR's election coverage in one place — from the biggest stories across the country, to the issues that matter close to home. Browse headlines, playlists, podcast episodes, videos and more, all on the 2026 Election tab.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has dismissed Army Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia, who oversaw planning at the Pentagon. Sylvia was also part of the Joint Chiefs of Staff. His removal comes as the U.S. and Israel prepare for a new potential round of attacks against Iran. Although Sylvia held a senior position in strategy, planning and policy, he was not directly involved in day-to-day operations regarding the Iran conflict.

  • 🎧 The Pentagon is investigating a leak but has not provided details, NPR's Greg Myre says. Hegseth has dismissed several generals and admirals, often without explanation. These firings have disrupted senior military operations, Myre says. The U.S. currently has two aircraft carriers in the Arabian Sea, with a third, the USS Theodore Roosevelt, en route. According to Myre, it is unusual for the U.S. to have multiple carriers in one region. The last time it stationed three in the Middle East was during the 2003 invasion of Iraq.

Thousands of military veterans with VA-backed mortgages have faced higher interest rates and monthly payments since last year, after the Trump administration shut down a key part of the VA's home loan program. Before it was shut down, the Veterans Affairs Servicing Purchase (VASP) program, created under the Biden administration, helped tens of thousands of veterans who had fallen behind on their payments by rolling missed payments into a new, low-interest mortgage. The mortgage industry and housing groups warned the administration not to kill the program without first creating a viable replacement. Without one, vets had to modify loans at higher interest rates. An NPR investigation found that more than 15,000 veterans experienced monthly payment increases of at least $150 after their loans were modified due to financial hardship. More than 700 veterans saw their payments rise by $1,000 or more.

Behind the story

by Rob Stein, NPR's science desk correspondent and senior editor

I've been doing stories about the organ transplantation system for decades. One of the most fundamental guiding ethical principles in organ donation has long been the "dead donor rule." That rule, stated simply, says: Organs should only be retrieved for transplants from a person who is dead, and death should never be accelerated to try to boost the chances their organs will be usable. To make sure that's the case, there's long been a strict firewall between the doctors and nurses trying to save patients in the hospital, and the organ retrieval teams standing by to try to procure their organs.

But over the years, I've heard many stories from family members who nevertheless felt pressured to donate their loved one's organs. So when I got a tip that the Organ Procurement & Transplantation Network, which runs the nation's organ system, was planning to relax that firewall, I instantly knew that was a big story.

I rushed to confirm the documentation that the network's board of directors had indeed endorsed the change, which would go into effect Nov. 18. I then reached out to bioethicists and others for their reaction to this major change. The revision was part of a set of new policies designed to boost donations and improve patient safety. Those changes were spurred by disturbing revelations about mistakes, including patients literally being wheeled into the operating room to remove their organs when they were still alive. Some of the changes were praised as improving safety. But many bioethicists and even some transplant surgeons and patient and organ donation advocates say relaxing the firewall between care and organ retrieval teams is dangerous. The fear is it could lead to families and caregivers discontinuing treatment too soon, and deepening distrust in the organ donation system.

I explored what these rule changes will mean for organ donors. You can read about it here.

Weekend picks

Check out what NPR is watching, reading and listening to this weekend:

🍿 Movies: It's officially Halloweekend a.k.a. the perfect time to watch a horror movie. Clayface embraces body horror to tell the origin story of the eponymous Batman villain. Tom Rhys Harries stars as an actor who turns to AI and nanotechnology for a radical solution after a mob boss disfigures him.

📺 TV: HBO's War features Dominic West and Sienna Miller as a British couple battling it out in a high-stakes divorce. Their fierce legal teams intensify the drama.

📚 Books: Elizabeth McCracken's Seven Stories About Tammy weaves together interconnected short stories about a family's experiences with the eldest son's girlfriend.

🎵 Music: Slovakian singer Adéla has spent her life preparing for pop stardom. She has recently gained attention with her hit song "Nicole Kidman." In this interview with NPR's World Cafe, she discusses the music industry and her debut album, PRIMA.

❓ Quiz: This week brought pre-midterm drama. Plus, the rest of the world also held elections. Stay sharp — you'll nail at least three questions.

3 things to know before you go

  • Sir Patrick Stewart, who played Professor X in the X-Men franchise and the captain of the starship USS Enterprise on Star Trek: The Next Generation, died on Wednesday at 86.
  • A new study in Science shows that a species of bird called the Manx shearwater experiences jet lag similar to humans. Researchers found that during long flights across the Atlantic, these birds become disoriented as their internal clock falls out of sync with the sun.
  • In this week's installment of Far-Flung Postcards, NPR's Jane Arraf sends greetings from the former home of English mystery novelist Agatha Christie, located on the banks of the Tigris River in Baghdad. The house now stands abandoned and crumbling.

This newsletter was edited by Suzanne Nuyen.

entries.title: The two most interesting risks to Anthropic
entries.summary: Anthropic gave a 94-page list of risk factors in its S-1 this week. Two of them stood out.
entries.content:
The two most interesting risks to Anthropic

You're reading a newsletter from The Indicator from Planet Money. Once a week, we curate our favorite stories and insights on business, finance, economics and why they matter. Subscribe here to get it in your inbox every Friday.

A TILE GAME is giving a boost to Chinese factories. Our very own Jennifer Pak reported that Chinese manufacturers have not had the easiest few years with U.S. tariffs and the war in Iran pushing up costs. Well, the aged game of Mahjong is giving them a surprising boost. That's because it's having a moment in the U.S. and some entrepreneurial citizens in China are enjoying the benefits. Mahjong sets can sell for like $300-$400 in the States … and want to know how much they cost to make? ~$30. One businessman said he used to make the game primarily for Chinese consumers. Now, every set is exported to the U.S.

Coming up:

  • The risks to Anthropic's (and AI's) business
  • Why we're saying 'buyout' and not 'layoff'
  • How young people are doing with AI summaries

New's We're Watching

The two most interesting risks to Anthropic - U.S. Securities & Exchange Commission

What to Know: Anthropic gave the world 94 pages of risks to its business (slash the entire AI economy) in its IPO prospectus aka the S-1. It wouldn't be Anthropic if they didn't discuss the "existential risks" to humanity and society several times. And isn't that an important risk to disclose? Another that stood out: the AI boom has a glaring point of failure. The majority of advanced semiconductor manufacturing is concentrated in one place, Taiwan, and if anything were to happen there, it could disrupt the entire AI economy. Think earthquake, Chinese military action, blockades. But I want to focus on a different risk, because it is FASCINATING!

Committing to the past at a premium: Anthropic is worried about aging out of the tech that's powering its AI, while paying the same prices. What does that mean?! AI companies have to lock into pricey contracts for all sorts of softwares, hardware, data center, and squadrons of GPUs. But technology is advancing quickly right now. New GPUs, for example, could come along that can do the same amount of work for way less money. Then Anthropic is stuck like CHUMPS in a contract paying a premium for old hardware, while some competitors may be doing more for less.

Why buyouts and not layoffs? - The Wall Street Journal

What To Know: Microsoft offered buyouts to 60,000 employees, roughly a quarter of its staff this week. And doesn't that sound better than "Microsoft laid off 60,000 employees this week"?? Skydance ALSO offered a buyout to employees on Monday, though it's not clear how many would be eligible. And here at NPR, we've been a fan of the term buyout too. So what's the real difference in offering a buyout versus just laying off staffers?

The difference: Morale? Morale. There's something about a "mega-layoff" that doesn't inspire worker confidence. A "buyout" not so much. Really? Ok, I guess. The WSJ reported the focus in C-suite land is on the ratio of employees to AI agents inside companies. Companies have to find ways to pay for the ever-increasing costs of AI … and you know … actual human workers expect to be paid.

Andy Challenger, Chief Revenue Officer of Challenger, Gray & Christmas, a consulting firm, told the Journal that it can help staffers emotionally by making it a little easier to let go. It also tends to motivate older staffers to retire a little bit early, which may be the company's goal.

Today's Indicator

There are more bots than humans online. Here's what that means

If you HAVEN'T listened: I never thought I'd yearn for the days when the internet felt wholesome. Where you could go to blogs and random sites and make friends across the world. Well, more than half of internet traffic now comes from non-humans, aka bots. They're pouring into the digital veins of the World Wide Web, ignoring a lot of ads, generating all kinds of comments, nonsense and what have you. One interesting takeaway: this shift from human-to-bot traffic changes the business model of the internet. If humans let bots do their shopping for them, then ads suddenly become less useful. And if ads don't pay out for websites, then who pays for them?

If you HAVE listened: Writer and researcher Erin Kissane says she believes Dead Internet Theory came out of a human impulse to "create speculative fiction versions" of real-life societal change that scares us. As a reminder, Dead Internet Theory is the idea that the internet becomes just bots talking to other bots.They're pouring into the digital veins of the World Wide Web, ignoring a lot of ads, generating all kinds of comments, nonsense and what have you. One interesting takeaway: this shift from human-to-bot traffic changes the business model of the internet. If humans let bots do their shopping for them, then ads suddenly become less useful. And if ads don't pay out for websites, then who pays for them?

Rest of the Week

How Meta plans to win the AI race with a "free" product

The case for (and against) abolishing MBAs

How Montana hopes to end corporate money in politics

Listener Mailbag

Listener Marjorie Wilkinson-Gruber sent in a comment from Marion, Iowa

Context: Marjorie wrote this message in response to Monday's episode on a human-less internet! There's a summary of the episode just above this segment.

Comment: After listening to today's episode of The Indicator, I had to write y'all. I'm a substitute teacher for middle school students in a public school district. This district serves mostly upper middle class students. I recently had a class of 8th graders given a research assignment. Seems pretty easy (enter the topic in Google, read some websites) so I was surprised when students began complaining that "everything is blocked". Turns out the school district had turned off/blocked AI summaries on the student computers. The students had become so reliant on the summaries that about half the class was stumped on what to do without them. They then complained loudly about having to read multiple websites to find the information they needed. "You expect me to actually read these pages?!?" Pretty disheartening and hard not to blame Google for forcing AI on all users/introducing the summaries in the first place!

In Our Spare Time

Producer Corey Bridges is playing through NPR's gaming coverage

Just last week I completed the campaign for Gears of War: E-Day and I thought it was excellent. I've never been a huge Gears of War fan, but this game was absolutely gorgeous and super fun to play. Xbox has had it pretty rough in recent years, so it's encouraging to see them churn out a game of the year quality product like this.

I've also been playing the new Nintendo Switch Sports Resort entry which I highly recommend to people who were fans of Wii Sports back in the day. And then finally, I've been preparing for the Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake by actually trying to progress in my year-old Breath of the Wild save. All I gotta say is, my backlog is looking more daunting than ever.

NPR put out its "Best Games of 2026" list. NPR is one of more than 150 outlets polled in The Game Awards, which has yet to be released.

entries.title: Candy prices got you scared stiff? What to know about the cost of Halloween this year
entries.summary: Prices for candy, the most popular Halloween purchase, and gum have risen 7.7% in one year and are up more than 18% in two years, according to the latest federal data.
entries.content:
Candy prices got you scared stiff? What to know about the cost of Halloween this year

For people stocking up on candy this Halloween, it's a spooky season in the grocery store — and not in a fun way.

Prices for candy, the most popular Halloween purchase, and gum have risen 7.7% in one year and are up more than 18% in two years, according to the latest federal data. That's higher than the average rate of food inflation during that time.

One major culprit: chocolate. Drought and heavy rains in places like West Africa have hurt cocoa harvests in recent seasons and pushed up prices worldwide.

Global cocoa production is now rebounding, but that isn't much help to consumers preparing to hand out candy to peckish trick-or-treaters this weekend, according to David Branch, sector manager with the Wells Fargo Agri-Food Institute.

"The candy on the shelves right now — chocolate candy — that cocoa was purchased in 2025," he said. And last year's cocoa prices were high.

Still, rising consumer prices aren't expected to scare people away from celebrating the holiday, with the National Retail Federation estimating consumers will spend $13.5 billion on Halloween this year. That's a 3% annual increase and sets a record: $115 per person, which is 55 cents more than last year.

Hair-raising cocoa prices are moderating

There was a surplus in the global supply of beans earlier this year, and cocoa prices have come down from their recent highs..

Yet Branch said consumer chocolate prices are "sticky," meaning they won't fall even when cocoa prices do because of the lag time in production. Manufacturers are also dealing with higher prices on other ingredients like sugar, pricier fuel costs due to the war in Iran and costlier imports subject to U.S. tariffs.

Enna Grazier, who owns the New Hampshire small-batch chocolate company Enna Chocolate, said she is facing a slew of higher costs, including a 50% tariff on some of the holiday packaging and ingredients she planned to purchase from Canadian suppliers.

"I've had to look elsewhere or get creative with some of my packaging needs for this holiday season, and that's super frustrating," Grazier said. "It's meant that I can't plan as far out, or the plans that I did make were disrupted and we've had to pivot and change."

Some candy makers have ushered in a flavor shift in recent years. Companies are offering more gummy and sour candy, and launching products that don't use pricier chocolate, such as KitKat's marshmallow-flavored Witch's Brew and Reese's White Ghosts coated in white creme.

Still, consumer demand for chocolate hasn't melted away. According to data from the market research firm Circana, which tracks purchases in U.S. supermarkets, chocolate candy sales have been increasing for several years running. However, shoppers have been buying less chocolate candy over the same period, which means people are paying more for chocolate and getting less of it.

entries.title: 'Affordability? For who?' Voters decide between helping homeowners or public services
entries.summary: Candidates across the U.S. have paid lip service to affordability issues. In Florida, the question of how to save voters money, and at what cost, is literally on the ballot.
entries.content:
'Affordability? For who?' Voters decide between helping homeowners or public services

JACKSONVILLE, Fla. – The ramp was steeper than she expected, but Rachel Dues was not going to stop. Not mere steps away from what she believed to be the most important thing she would do this year.

Dues, 54, gathered herself then pushed hard, propelling the wheelchair that carried her injured niece to the polls.

"You're gonna get in there. I don't care how," Dues said, her voice breathless with effort. She was speaking as much to herself as she was to her niece, 21-year-old Rochelle Covington, who asked to come along to vote.

"By any means necessary," Dues said, giving the wheelchair another shove.

For Dues, this year's midterm election feels existential. Gas prices have soared, her rent is up, and some days it feels like simply buying groceries or paying her electricity bill could push her over budget.

While political candidates all over the country have paid lip service to issues of affordability, here in Florida, the question of how to make life more affordable is literally on the ballot.

A massive property tax cut has been put to voters in the form of Amendment 3, a ballot measure that asks Florida residents to vote on increasing the amount of money that can be exempted from homestead taxes. The proposal would increase the allowable amount from $50,000 to as much as $250,000 over the next two years, cutting billions of dollars in revenue from local governments' budgets. If the measure passes, some jurisdictions could functionally eliminate all non-school homestead property taxes over time.

That could mean thousands of dollars in annual savings for some homeowners — something supporters have called a game-changer for Florida residents stretched thin by a strained economy. But in an already tax-averse state — Florida famously does not have individual income or estate taxes, among others — local governments have limited revenue streams from which to pull funds for public services, and property taxes have been a lifeline.

Critics have cautioned that the proposed tax exemption will have dire consequences: cuts to public services and infrastructure, eroded social safety net programs and a domino effect that could drive up costs elsewhere should city and county governments attempt to recoup lost revenue.

"One of the things our members are always knocking on doors and asking is: affordability? For who?" said Steven Johnson, an organizer with grassroots nonprofit Florida Rising, which organizes residents to get involved in political action on state and local issues.

Florida isn't the only place where politicians have explored ways to cut, or even eliminate, property taxes — 11 states have reined in property taxes so far in 2026, according to an analysis by the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities. But Florida's proposal, which is more expansive than many others, puts the question directly to voters.

How they vote, experts said, could set the stage for what's to come in Florida and around the nation.

A disabled veteran, Dues works as a notary and closing agent on home sales. For her, she said, the Amendment 3 vote is personal.

"Lucky for me I'm a resourceful person, but I rely on things like food pantries and other services to get by," Dues said. "Now I'm wondering, what am I going to do if they get rid of all that? What can I do?"

The impact

Since it was introduced, Florida's proposed Amendment 3 has been pitched to voters as an affordability fix for homeowners.

While the state already has laws limiting how much can be taxed of a home's assessed value — and how much that amount can grow each year — this amendment would, in some cases, virtually eliminate all property taxes due on a homeowner's primary residence.

Backers like Florida's Republican governor, Ron DeSantis, and the Florida Realtors trade association have said property taxes have grown out of control and local governments are flush with excess revenue as a result.

"Homeowners have funded the incredible increase in revenue that is now at record growth, and as property values have increased that growth has translated into significant revenue gains for local governments," said Margy Grant, the CEO of Florida Realtors, which as of the end of October put $19.5 million into the 'Vote Yes on 3' campaign. "This is about making sure that Floridians who want to stay in their homes and are seeing this rising cost get to stay in their homes."

In the campaign to persuade Floridians to vote yes, ads highlight just how expensive daily life has gotten.

"Everything keeps going up!" the Vote Yes on 3 website exclaims. "Cost of living. Inflation. PROPERTY TAXES. What if there was a SOLUTION that could help?"

"Florida families are paying more for nearly everything, whether it's groceries, fuel, insurance, utilities and housing," Grant said. "This is tax relief money that stays in a Floridian's pocket instead of going to the government."

Property tax revenue collected by local governments in the state has nearly doubled from around $32 billion in 2019 to almost $60 billion in the last fiscal year, according to the governor's office. Much of that growth, experts said, was driven by a post-pandemic real estate boom with out-of-state residents moving in and low interest rates driving new property sales.

The question of how law enforcement, fire and emergency medical services will be affected by these potential tax cuts have fueled headline-grabbing debates across the state. Some public officials have insisted emergency services will be able to weather any cuts, while others, including the Florida Sheriffs Association, warned they would suffer.

Amendment 3 proponents said these warnings have been overblown.

"That is just a talking point of the opposition," Grant said.

Sen. Rick Scott (R-Fla.), who supports the measure, wrote in a post on X that "every county has waste to cut," and argued that the amendment would force local governments to eliminate waste rather than essential services.

But local leaders said services other than police, fire and EMS are likely to be hit even harder: Funds for libraries, public transportation, infrastructure, homelessness prevention, small business supports, after-school programs for kids and more could be eliminated.

The amendment was put to voters "very, very quickly and without understanding the unintended consequences," said Mike Weinstein, Jacksonville's chief administrative officer and a former state legislator. "There's a small segment of homeowners that will benefit from this. But the majority of people — renters, business owners, everyone else, and even many homeowners — won't see any benefit from this amendment at all." (The amendment would limit which homeowners qualify for the increased exemption based on when they purchased their home.)

According to an analysis by the state's Office of Economic and Demographic Research, the amendment would cut local revenue in the state by nearly $12 billion on a recurring basis. In Jacksonville, the Florida Policy Institute found, that could mean losing as much as $372 million over the next five years.

"Our budget here is $2 billion. A billion comes from property taxes," Weinstein said. "So, mosquito control, road surfacing, libraries, parks, all will be affected. And so will police and fire."

Weinstein, a Republican, said in lieu of funding things like parks and libraries, fixing roads or clearing trash, the city may instead have to channel resources toward opening a "very big" complaints department.

Getting out the vote

Maggie Fernandez, 68, is exactly the kind of person who might benefit from Amendment 3. She owns her own home. Her husband is retired.

But in recent weeks, Fernandez has spent her nights and weekends in the lead up to Election Day phone banking and knocking on doors to get her neighbors to vote the amendment down.

"Sure, I might see some relief in taxes," Fernandez said. "But overall this is going to hurt local services. It's going to hurt people who are worse off than we are."

Fernandez signed up to do voter outreach with Florida Rising. On a recent weekday evening, she was one of more than a dozen volunteers who packed into the progressive nonprofit's office and hit the phones. All told, organizers said, they made nearly 1,500 calls that night.

With early voting already underway in Florida, Fernandez said she felt a renewed sense of urgency to get the "vote no" message out.

She dialed number after number — 111 in one night — leaving messages and urging those who answered to consider how Amendment 3 might hurt their neighbors in the long run.

Down the hall, Dues was also making calls.

When a woman answered halfway through the evening, Dues scrambled for her script.

"Amendment 3 may lead to cuts on local services like flood prevention, road maintenance, public transportation and housing assistance and that's what it doesn't tell you when you see those commercials on TV," Dues said. "It doesn't tell you any of that, it just makes you think it's this great amendment."

The woman on the other line said she'd be voting no.

Dues exhaled as she hung up the phone.

'People don't know'

Dues doesn't need to work hard to picture how the amendment might affect her daily life. She thinks about it constantly: On her drives across town as she calculates the amount of gas it might take to get home; on her regular visits to food pantries, where she gathers enough bread and eggs and frozen meat to make it through the month.

Will the food banks be able to operate if they lose city funding, she wonders. Will relief programs that help renters like her pay for utility bills or avoid eviction disappear?

In her work as a closing agent, Dues sees how much people are paying to become homeowners in Florida, and, she said, she feels for anyone who is struggling to make ends meet.

But she's done her research and practiced her pitch. Whenever she gets the chance, she tells homeowners that the affordability Amendment 3 promises isn't all it's cracked up to be.

"When I first heard about it, I was like, oh that's great. That'll really help people," Dues said. "But then I learned more about it and it felt like a bait and switch. It might be great for some people, in the short term, but in the long run, it's going to do a lot of harm."

If local lawmakers shift the financial burden into other taxes homeowners could end up paying more in other places, she tells friends and colleagues.

Renters like her, she says, may absorb increases put to landlords or commercial properties. And any programs that exist to help people survive won't necessarily be there to help anymore.

The amendment needs the approval of a supermajority — 60% or more — to pass.

On a recent morning outside a church on the west side of Jacksonville, Dues got in line to register for the food bank. She needed a few staples, she said, to carry her through the end of the month.

"Are you voting?" she asked the woman working the sign-in desk.

The volunteer squinted up at her.

"You know to vote 'no' on Amendment 3, right?" Dues pitched, taking a number.

Dues said she's never been more nervous before an election.

"It's kind of scary to me that people don't know" about the amendment, she said.

Looking around the crowd gathered for boxes of bread and other pantry items, Dues shook her head.

"How do they expect poor people to be able to live as regular people?" she wondered aloud.

The number in her hand read 104. All around her, the crowd was still growing.

entries.title: For voters from immigrant families and new citizens, voting is bigger than themselves
entries.summary: While many young voters are focused on the cost of living in the election, for some from immigrant families, the political calculation — and their votes — is often about even more than the economy.
entries.content:
For voters from immigrant families and new citizens, voting is bigger than themselves

Nicole Solis-Sison moved to America when she was seven years old. Her parents and immediate family were fleeing the Philippine government and sought asylum in the U.S.

When they landed in Los Angeles, Solis-Sison thought their stay would be temporary. Eventually, once things calmed down in her home country, they would return. That wasn't the case.

"The Philippine government pursued us in international immigration territory and demanded that we be sent back," she told NPR.

That's when an agent with the then-Immigration and Naturalization Services agency — which has since been renamed Immigration and Customs Enforcement, or ICE — showed up to her house. They were prepared to be deported. But after the agent interviewed her family, they weren't packing their bags back to Manila.

"This particular INS [Immigration and Naturalization Services] agent suggested that we should file for asylum, given that we were on U.S. soil," Solis-Sison said.

An immigration agent, Solis-Sison said, gave her family the tools needed to stay in the U.S. legally. Earlier this year, after more than two decades navigating the immigration system, she became an American citizen. Now, at the age of 34, Solis-Sison is voting in her very first election in New York City.

"This is like such a milestone year for me that I'm a first time voter. I created my own voter guide and voter diary," she said.

Many young voters, including Solis-Sison, are worried about their future. Will they be able to buy a home? How will they pay off their student loans? Is it economical to start a family?

But this midterm election, the motivation for voting is a little different for some young people with immigrant family members and for newly naturalized citizens.

Solis-Sison considers herself lucky. As she heads to the polls for the first time, she said her immigrant experience is informing her vote. She feels a responsibility.

"I feel like I do have a weight to protect people who are going through this process, who are getting left behind and harmed because when I tell you, I've only gotten out of it with like a sliver of hope," she said.

The power of voting

Juan Escalante didn't know he was undocumented growing up in south Florida.

Originally from Venezuela, his family moved to the states when he was 11 years old. He said he lived a normal life in America but that changed when he discovered he wasn't legally allowed to be in the U.S. around his junior year of high school.

"Basically, what ended up happening was that my parents paid for a lawyer who gave them really bad advice and not only gave them bad advice, but also mishandled their immigration case entirely," Escalante said.

He added when something happens like that, the immigration application can't simply be refiled, "you're kind of out of the line entirely." His immigration status changed under the Obama administration when the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals, or DACA, program was established.

Under the program, he became the first person in his family to graduate college. Then, in 2025, he became the first American citizen in his family. This year, at 37, he will vote in his first general election.

"Being a first time voter here in the United States is something that's profoundly personal and emotional for me because I understand the power of what a vote can do in service of the greater good, in service of the community, in service of the of the future that you want to see for your community, your state and your country."

"I'm proud to be an American citizen," Escalante said.

When he first received his mail-in ballot, Escalante had mixed emotions. He was thrilled to cast a vote, but as a California resident, he found himself overwhelmed by the sheer size of his ballot. But that didn't stop him from meticulously researching every last ballot proposition and candidate. To him, it's something he's worked the majority of his life for.

"Despite the amount of bubbles that I had to fill in and the amount of research that I had to do, I never once took that for granted as I was filling out my ballot," he said.

But he did want to make sure that his vote supported his family and community. Though his parents are both green card holders, he said it doesn't stop anyone in the family from worrying about their future status. So, when he was spending tons of time trying to figure out which politician to vote for, immigration was at the top of his mind.

"I do want to make sure that my values as an immigrant, as the first of my family to vote and also as a Latino to make sure that all of that is carried and translated through to my ballot," he said.

Mixed status families

24-year-old Deisy España of Wisconsin also feels the weight of her family's immigrant history. España is from a mixed-status family. While she was born in the U.S. and has always been a citizen, her parents are from Mexico. Growing up, both of her parents were undocumented.

España said she didn't understand the risks to her parents when she was younger, like when her parents got pulled over by the police while driving.

"My mom would start, like, doing the sign of the cross or praying and I never understood what that fear was until I got much older and realized that they were scared that they were going to get turned over to ICE," she said.

Some of that has changed. Her mom recently obtained a green card. But the fear hasn't completely dissipated. ICE has been in the news a lot since President Trump returned to office. Every time España encounters someone whose family member has been taken by ICE, or reads about an ICE related death, the same thing runs through her head.

"That could have been my dad," she said.

Immigration policy has always been a priority for España and she has always been politically active, despite not being old enough to vote until 2020. But she said more feels at risk this election, especially with Trump's hardline stance on immigration and ICE agents arresting people who look like her parents. España said she carries more than just her views into the ballot box.

"I'm voting for my parents. I have to do it for my parents who can't vote. But even now, more than ever," España said.

That has been España's message for other young voters with immigrant families. Don't vote for yourself. Vote for your parents.

23-year-old Leydi Gonzalez of Texas is in a similar position as España. While she is an American citizen, both of Gonzalez's parents are from El Savador. She said the number one thing she was looking forward to once she turned 21 years old was helping her parents gain legal status.

"When I turned 21, the first thing that I was excited for was to finally petition my parents. It wasn't drinking," she said.

Now, thanks to Gonzalez's sponsorship, they have authorization to be in the U.S. They're in the system and crossing their fingers for residency approval.

While there is a layer of legal protection for her parents, Gonzalez is still worried something could happen. Gonzalez said her family started having conversations about who would take care of her siblings if her parents were detained or deported when Trump was first elected president.

"That is a scary conversation to have. Like, 'Hey, just in case something unknown happens to your parents, this is who you're gonna be left with,'" Gonzalez explained.

Now, she feels like the stakes are just as high, if not higher. Her community has been rocked by the killing of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Texas by an ICE agent. But she does think things are on the precipice of change this election, especially if control of Congress changes.

It's playing out in her backyard. There is a high profile U.S. Senate race in Texas. While Texas is a reliably red state, Democrat James Talarico has been polling ahead of Republican nominee, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton.

She said she is voting for her best interest, but it is bigger than that.

"It definitely feels like I'm voting for my family," Gonzalez said. " Definitely a sense of security for my family."

entries.title: Here are the Senate races to watch ahead of Election Day
entries.summary: The competitive map for control of the U.S. Senate has expanded considerably in the final days before Election Day. Here's a ranking of those competitive races from most likely to flip to least likely.
entries.content:
Here are the Senate races to watch ahead of Election Day

📲 Get the latest on the midterms & more in the NPR App

When this election cycle began, Democrats were seen as a longshot to pick up the Senate.

That's because so many seats that are up for election are in red states. But as the year has gone on and the war in Iran has continued, the field has widened considerably.

Polling, ad money and candidate and surrogate travel have all indicated competitive races in places Trump won by double digits in 2024. Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Ohio and Texas are all considered Toss Ups, according to the Cook Political Report.

"I'm very energized," said Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, D-N.Y., chairwoman of the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, which is charged with trying to elect Democrats to the Senate. "We have so many candidates running in so many deep red and purple places, and they are winning, and it is exciting. People want change, and we have so much talent on the field right now. I feel very inspired."

The races in all of these competitive states where Trump won are within the margin of error.

Republicans have a decidedly different view.

"Senate Democrats' socialist surge has reached a fever pitch, and their desperate conspiracies to defraud voters appear criminal," said Bernadette Breslin, national press secretary for the National Republican Senatorial Committee, the counterpart to the DSCC.

She's referring to a controversy in the Alaska Senate race about the alleged involvement of members of the campaign for the Democratic candidate, Mary Peltola, to recruit Daniel J. Sullivan to run, as first reported by The New York Times. The incumbent Republican is named Dan Sullivan.

"Common-sense voters across red-leaning battlegrounds are preparing to reject the dangerously unaffordable agendas of Abdul El-Sayed [in Michigan], Troy Jackson [in Maine], and Mary Peltola—along with the Democrat Party's dying brand."

But showing the direction the winds have been blowing, North Carolina, where Trump won narrowly, and was seen as a Toss Up race at the beginning of this cycle, is now seen as a likely flip for Democrats. And Georgia, once thought to be a top Republican target, is now a likely hold for Democrats.

Even South Carolina, a place Trump won by 18 points, is only leaning toward the Republican Party. Mississippi and Nebraska are also more competitive than Republicans would like, but GOP candidates are favored there.

Democrats need to flip a net of four seats held by Republicans to win control of the Senate. And while the field is wide for Democrats, winning control is hardly a done deal. Republicans have a few targets on the board still, principally in Michigan, but also New Hampshire and Minnesota. Winning even one of those seriously complicates Democrats' math.

The key to whether the Democrats win the Senate and how big the Democratic wave is, if there is one at all, is likely to be Republican turnout. Low GOP turnout could mean the difference between Democrats netting one or two seats and picking up six or seven.

Loading...

Let's take a look at the competitive states and where things stand, rated by tiers.

Tiers below are in order of most to least likely to flip. Within tiers, they are in alphabetical order. Ratings are based on the Cook Political Report:

Tier 1: NC (R)

Tier 2: MI (D), OH (R)

Tier 3: AK (R), ME (R), IA (R), TX (R)

Tier 4: KS (R), NH (D), SC (R), MN (D)

Tier 5: MS (R), NE (R), GA (D)

TIER 1: NC

NORTH CAROLINA (R-OPEN-Tillis retiring) — LIKELY D

Both parties concede former Gov. Roy Cooper is likely to be the next senator from the state — even President Trump apparently thinks so. "He's going to become your senator," Trump said during a stop in North Carolina earlier this month, "and it's crazy." 2024: TRUMP +3

TIER 2: MI (D), OH (R)

MICHIGAN (D-OPEN-Peters retiring) — TOSS UP

Republicans' best pick-up opportunity, this race will test whether a bold progressive can win in a purple state with Democrat Abdul El-Sayed's candidacy. But also factoring in here is former moderate Rep. Mike Rogers' (R) turn to MAGA and use of racist attacks to try and win. 2024: TRUMP +1

OHIO (R-Husted) — TOSS UP

Sherrod Brown's (D) decision to try for a comeback after being ousted in 2024 turned this race on its head. He's the challenger, but with his high name recognition and time in the Senate, Republicans have treated him as an incumbent. Trump has tried to boost incumbent Sen. John Husted (R) in recent weeks with explicit comments on his physique. But the issues here have Republicans on the defensive — the economy, gas prices and AI data center growth have given Democrats an opening for a pathway back in a state Trump has won three times. 2024: TRUMP +11

TIER 3: AK (R), IA (R), ME (R), TX (R)

ALASKA (R-Sullivan) — TOSS UP

The hijinks and misinformation ahead of the election here underscore that state's importance. Peltola appeared to have the inside track, but the late recruiting scandal threatens to derail that momentum. 2024: TRUMP +14

IOWA (R-OPEN-Ernst) — TOSS UP

From the governor's race down to the Senate and House race, Iowa looks poised to move left this cycle. Democrat Josh Turek is in a tight race with Trump-backed Rep. Ashley Hinson (R). Tariffs, the war and rising diesel prices have hurt the agricultural economy here and put Republicans on their heels. Plus, Democrats could get be helped by the gubernatorial run of Rob Sand (D), who has run one of the best campaigns of any candidate in the country. 2024: TRUMP +13

MAINE (R-Collins) — TOSS UP

Can Sen. Susan Collins (R) survive again? Polls showed her losing in 2020 and she gutted out a win. The race is tight, and Collins appears to be holding up, but the Democratic base of voters in the only Toss Up state won by Kamala Harris (D) in 2024, gives Troy Jackson (D) a real shot here. 2024: HARRIS +6

TEXAS (R-OPEN-Cornyn lost primary) — TOSS UP

It's hard to see Republicans flipping Michigan and losing Texas, but because of candidate quality in both places, it's possible. State Rep. James Talarico would have probably had a much harder time against incumbent Sen. John Cornyn, but Trump decided to endorse the more MAGA-aligned — and scandal-ridden — state Attorney General Ken Paxton in the primary runoff. That has led to a Brinks truck being backed up into the state of Texas. More than $500 million has been spent on this race since the primary, more than $300 million of that from Republicans. Democrats haven't won statewide in Texas since 1994, there are lots of Republicans here, and Democrats have continued to come up short in recent years even with high levels of enthusiasm, so there's a healthy dose of "believe-it-when-I-see-it" skepticism here. But one thing to consider is that in 2018 when Democrat Beto O'Rourke lost to incumbent Sen. Ted Cruz by less than 3 points, he never led in a single poll. This time around, Talarico has led in almost every one, even if those leads have been within the margin of error. Something to watch: whether Gina Hinojosa's (D) gubernatorial campaign gets close and turns out big numbers of Latinos in South Texas. That could help Talarico over the finish line. 2024: TRUMP +13

Loading...

TIER 4: KS (R), MN (D), NH (D), SC (R)

KANSAS — TOSS UP (R-Marshall)

Not all Toss Ups are created equal. This has been a surprisingly close race for incumbent Sen. Roger Marshall (R). He's facing a strong challenger in pastor Adam Hamilton and political headwinds because of Trump's policies' effect on the state's economy. Republicans insist Marshall will pull it off at the end of the day and note that Marshall's last race was closer than the lean of the state, too. This is a Toss Up, but the heavy Republican lean of the state makes this one seem less likely for Democrats, but wild things happen in wave years. 2024: TRUMP +16

MINNESOTA (D-OPEN-Klobuchar ran for governor) — LEAN D

One of only three states won by Harris in 2024, and in a year favoring Democrats, Minnesota is perhaps a surprise to be moving more in Republicans' direction in the final days. But Republicans have been trying to peg the lapses in state oversight for a Medicare fraud scandal to Democratic nominee Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan. Plus, Republicans like the race former NFL reporter Michelle Tafoya has been running. This may be a state that tends to vote Democratic but this a place that Hillary Clinton (D) only won by less than 2 points and Harris only won by 4. At the end of the day, the advantage still goes to Democrats here, but it doesn't mean they won't sweat. 2024: HARRIS +4

NEW HAMPSHIRE (D-OPEN-Shaheen retiring) — LEAN D

This has been a top Republican target since the beginning of the cycle when they felt they got a big recruiting win with former Sen. Jon Sununu. And they're hoping for a down-ballot effect with former Republican Sen. Kelly Ayotte favored to win the governorship. But the national political winds still mean Rep. Chris Pappas (D) is the slight favorite. 2024: HARRIS +3

SOUTH CAROLINA (R-OPEN-Graham died) — LEAN R

That this one is even being talked about is remarkable. Trump won here by 18 points in 2024 and Sen. Lindsey Graham was heavily favored before his untimely death. Trump pushed for Graham's sister, Darline, to take the seat, but she's a political novice and has been getting swamped on the air with ads boosting Democratic nominee Annie Andrews. Republicans have the edge because of the lean of the state but watch Black turnout here. If it's presidential-level high, Democrats could have a shot. 2024: TRUMP +18

Tier 5: MS (R), NE (R), GA (D)

MISSISSIPPI (R-Hyde-Smith) — LIKELY R

Democrats have been saying for months that this one could be competitive if the political winds get even stronger. That's happened, and they like their candidate. But it would be a shocker if this state that went by more than 20 points for Trump flipped. It's heavily Republican despite its large Black population because white voters vote in extraordinarily high numbers for Republicans here. 2024: TRUMP +22

NEBRASKA (R-Ricketts) — LIKELY R

No one is surprised this cycle by Dan Osborn's independent candidacy. So Republicans are confident this one stays in their hands. But Osborn making this a race at all is an indication of the difficult national environment for Republicans and the kinds of non-GOP candidates that can have an appeal in red states. It's also an example of how bad the Democratic brand is in some of these places, too. 2024: TRUMP +20

GEORGIA (D-Ossoff) — LIKELY D

This was supposed to be a top GOP target but Ossoff's candidacy and his war chest have made him the heavy favorite. Once this one's official, the political world will be waiting for the launch of the Ossoff 2028 campaign. 2024: TRUMP +2
